title: Excessive disclosure of homeowner identity and household details during registration
description: During account registration and device enrollment, the homeowner may be required to provide more personal data than is necessary for initial setup, such as full identity, precise address, household composition, or unnecessary profile attributes. The act of sharing this data from the homeowner to the Home Hub creates a disclosure risk.
assumptions: Assumes the registration/enrollment flow requests personal and household information beyond the minimum needed to create the account and pair devices.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-effort because the retrieved context did not include detailed threat-tree nodes for disclosure.

title: Linkability of homeowner identity with enrolled device identifiers in transit
description: The registration/enrollment flow can carry both account identifiers and camera/sensor identifiers or serial numbers. If these are observable together on the flow, they can enable linking a specific person or household to a set of devices and, by extension, to a smart-home installation.
assumptions: Assumes the flow contains both user/account data and device identifiers, and that metadata or payload contents are observable on the communication path.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; context only confirmed that Linkability is applicable for ExternalEntity->Process flows.

title: Identifiability of the homeowner from registration payload or communication metadata
description: Personally identifying information in the registration payload, or metadata such as network identifiers associated with the enrollment session, may allow an observer to identify the homeowner or household initiating setup.
assumptions: Assumes the flow includes direct identifiers (e.g., email, username) or indirectly identifying metadata (e.g., IP address, stable device identifiers).
uncertainty_note: Exact tree node is approximate due to limited retrieved threat-tree detail.

title: Home Hub stores registration and enrollment data more broadly than necessary
description: Once received, the Home Hub may retain account details, device serial numbers, pairing history, and household configuration in a way that exposes more personal information than needed for operation. This creates a disclosure threat at the destination because the recipient's processing and storage practices cause the privacy risk.
assumptions: Assumes the Home Hub persists registration and enrollment data locally or forwards it for storage without strict data minimization.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is approximate; detailed disclosure subnodes were not provided in the retrieved context.

title: Insufficient transparency about how registration and device-enrollment data will be used
description: The Home Hub may collect account and device-enrollment data without clearly informing the homeowner how the data will be used, retained, shared, or combined with other smart-home data. This creates an unawareness threat at the destination because the recipient's collection interface and processing may not provide adequate notice.
assumptions: Assumes the setup process does not clearly explain purposes, retention, recipients, or downstream processing of registration and enrollment data.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; applicability is strong but retrieved context lacked detailed U threat-tree nodes.

title: Registration and enrollment proceed without valid or granular consent
description: The Home Hub may bundle account creation, device enrollment, analytics, cloud synchronization, or data sharing into a single acceptance step, preventing the homeowner from giving specific and freely given consent for each purpose. This creates a non-compliance risk at the destination.
assumptions: Assumes consent is relied upon as a legal basis for some processing and that setup does not provide purpose-specific choices.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; legal basis depends on system context and jurisdiction.

title: Temporary access code can identify or single out a guest in transit
description: The temporary access code transmitted from the guest to the Home Hub may act as a unique token tied to a specific guest invitation or visit window. Anyone able to observe the flow, or metadata associated with it, could single out that guest interaction or infer which guest is attempting entry.
assumptions: Assumes the temporary code is unique per guest, visit, or time window, and that the communication can be observed locally or over a network/interface.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node selection is best-effort because the retrieved context did not include detailed I-subtree nodes.

title: Observation of unlock-code submission reveals guest participation
description: Even without learning the code value, observing that this flow occurs can reveal that a guest is currently attempting access to the home. Presence, timing, and repetition of code-entry events may disclose guest involvement or occupancy patterns.
assumptions: Assumes an attacker can observe the keypad interaction, local wireless signaling, or other side effects of the submission event.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node selection is approximate; the supplied context supports detecting via observed communication or side effects, but not a more specific subtree id.

title: Home Hub can link guest code use across visits or with other household events
description: If the Home Hub stores or correlates temporary access-code submissions with timestamps, door unlock events, device identifiers, or household logs, it may link multiple actions to the same guest or invitation. This can enable profiling of guest visits and behavior over time.
assumptions: Assumes the Home Hub logs code submissions or associates codes with guest identities, invitations, or other events.
uncertainty_note: Specific subtree id is best-effort due to missing detailed L threat-tree context.

title: Home Hub can identify the guest from the temporary code
description: On receipt, the Home Hub may resolve the temporary access code to a specific invited guest, household contact, or booking record. This turns the submitted code into directly identifying information about who is at the door.
assumptions: Assumes temporary codes are assigned per guest or can be mapped to a guest record.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node selection is approximate because detailed identification subtree nodes were not provided.

title: Guest code submission may be logged as evidence of entry attempt
description: The Home Hub may retain logs showing that a particular temporary code was entered at a specific time. Such records can later be used as evidence that the guest attempted access or entered the premises, reducing the guest's plausible deniability regarding participation.
assumptions: Assumes the hub logs successful or failed code-entry attempts with timestamps and code references.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node selection is best-effort due to absent detailed non-repudiation subtree mapping.

title: Stored access-attempt records expose guest presence patterns
description: By processing or storing temporary code submissions, the Home Hub can reveal whether a guest was present, when they arrived, and how often they attempted entry. Even if the guest is not explicitly named, these records may disclose participation in household activities.
assumptions: Assumes the hub stores access attempts or exposes them through dashboards, notifications, or integrations.
uncertainty_note: Specific D subtree id is approximate.

title: Temporary code handling may disclose sensitive guest-related information
description: If the Home Hub stores or exposes temporary codes, invitation labels, or associated notes, it may disclose private details such as who was invited, when access was granted, or special visit arrangements. Failed-attempt logs may also reveal that a guest was expected but could not enter.
assumptions: Assumes the hub persists code values or associated guest metadata and that these are accessible to household members, admins, or integrated services.
uncertainty_note: Detailed disclosure subtree node not available in retrieved context; node id is approximate.

title: Guest may be unaware of logging and secondary use of temporary code data
description: The Home Hub may process the temporary access code for purposes beyond immediate door unlocking, such as audit logging, analytics, notifications, or sharing with cloud services. If this is not transparent to the guest, the guest may be insufficiently informed about how their access event is used.
assumptions: Assumes the guest is not clearly informed at the point of entry about logging, retention, or onward sharing.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node selection is approximate because detailed unawareness subtree nodes were not provided.

title: Guest may have no meaningful choice or control over processing of access-event data
description: To gain entry, the guest must submit the temporary code to the Home Hub, but may have no practical way to object to logging, retention, or sharing of the resulting access-event data. This creates a privacy threat where participation is effectively conditioned on accepting downstream processing.
assumptions: Assumes no alternative entry method or privacy controls are offered to the guest regarding retention or sharing of access logs.
uncertainty_note: Specific non-compliance/control subtree node is best-effort; applicability depends on system policy and available guest choices.

title: Sensor-event records can link household behavior over time
description: By writing motion, door, and other sensor events into a persistent log, the Home Hub creates a longitudinal record that can be linked across time to the same household, enabling inference of routines, occupancy patterns, and relationships between events.
assumptions: Events are associated with a stable home, device, room, or account context so records can be correlated over time.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context only provided applicability by threat type, not detailed node ids.

title: Sensor events may identify residents through behavioral patterns
description: Even if the log stores only event data, combinations of timestamps, device identifiers, and event sequences may identify or single out residents by their distinctive movement and usage patterns.
assumptions: The event log contains timestamps and sensor/device context detailed enough to distinguish individuals or households.
uncertainty_note: Identification may be indirect via behavioral fingerprinting rather than explicit names.

title: Local event log stores intimate household activity data
description: The destination data store accumulates motion, door, and sensor events that reveal presence at home, sleep/wake cycles, room usage, and other private aspects of domestic life beyond what occupants may expect from simple device operation.
assumptions: The log is retained for some period and can be queried or inspected locally or by software on the hub.
uncertainty_note: Specific disclosure channel is not described, but the privacy risk arises from storing detailed activity history.

title: Persistent logging enables detection of habits and occupancy
description: Analysis of the stored event history can detect when occupants are home or away, daily routines, unusual absences, and other sensitive patterns from repeated sensor activations.
assumptions: Historical events are retained with timestamps and are accessible for analysis by the system or an authorized party.
uncertainty_note: This is a classic detectability/inference risk from retained telemetry; exact node id is approximate.

title: Residents may be unaware of the extent of local event logging
description: If the system logs all motion, door, and sensor events locally without clear notice, occupants may not understand that detailed behavioral data is being recorded and retained, undermining transparency.
assumptions: User-facing setup or documentation does not fully explain the scope, granularity, or retention of local logs.
uncertainty_note: Applies if transparency about local logging is insufficient; the flow description alone does not confirm notice mechanisms.

title: Local retention of sensor-event history may exceed consent or expected purpose
description: Writing detailed household sensor events to a local log may go beyond the purpose users consented to if logging is broader, longer, or more reusable than needed for immediate device functionality.
assumptions: Consent, configuration, or legitimate-purpose boundaries for logging are limited or not explicit.
uncertainty_note: This depends on the product's consent and purpose specification, which are not provided.

title: Uploading recorded clips discloses highly sensitive in-home activity to a third party
description: The Home Hub shares recorded camera clips with cloud storage. Video from inside or around a home can reveal occupants, visitors, routines, possessions, and special-category inferences, so the act of sending the clips off-device creates a disclosure risk beyond local processing.
assumptions: Assumes clips contain identifiable people or household context and are transmitted to infrastructure outside the user's immediate control.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort based on generic disclosure-at-source semantics; exact subnode may differ in the full LINDDUN Pro tree.

title: Upload traffic metadata can link clips to a specific household or device
description: Even if clip contents are protected, the flow itself may expose stable identifiers or metadata such as device IDs, account identifiers, IP address, timing, and upload frequency. These can link multiple uploads to the same home, user account, or camera over time.
assumptions: Assumes network or application-layer metadata is observable to intermediaries or the cloud provider and contains stable or correlatable identifiers.
uncertainty_note: Exact LINDDUN Pro subnode for metadata-based linkability may vary.

title: Upload metadata can identify the household behind the camera clips
description: Network and application metadata in transit, such as subscriber/account identifiers, IP address, device serials, or camera IDs, may allow the uploader or household to be identified even without inspecting the video payload.
assumptions: Assumes identifiers are present in protocol headers, authentication context, or observable side channels.
uncertainty_note: Best-effort generic identifiability node; exact subnode may differ.

title: Clip contents or metadata may be exposed in transit
description: If transport protection is weak, misconfigured, or terminated in untrusted infrastructure, the uploaded video clips or associated metadata may be disclosed during transmission to cloud storage.
assumptions: Assumes imperfect transport security or exposure at proxies, gateways, or monitoring points.
uncertainty_note: Applies only if in-transit protections are insufficient; if strong end-to-end protections are assured, likelihood would be lower.

title: Cloud storage can link uploaded clips across time, cameras, and accounts
description: Once received, the cloud video store can correlate clips by account, device, timestamps, location, and other metadata, enabling construction of a longitudinal profile of household behavior and relationships between cameras or users.
assumptions: Assumes the datastore retains identifiers and metadata alongside clips.
uncertainty_note: Exact subnode may differ; threat is grounded in recipient-side correlation.

title: Stored clips and metadata can identify residents, visitors, and the household
description: The destination can identify data subjects directly from video imagery, voices, faces, surroundings, account data, and device metadata, turning uploaded clips into identified or identifiable personal data.
assumptions: Assumes the cloud service has access to clip contents and associated account/device metadata.
uncertainty_note: Generic identifiability node used as best fit.

title: Cloud retention and access to clips causes disclosure of private home life
description: At the destination, storing and processing the uploaded clips creates risk that provider personnel, subprocessors, attackers, or overbroad integrations gain access to intimate footage and household information.
assumptions: Assumes clips are retained in readable form or accessible after decryption within the cloud service.
uncertainty_note: Best-effort disclosure node; exact subnode may differ.

title: Cloud analysis of uploaded clips enables surveillance of household behavior
description: The recipient can analyze stored video to infer occupancy patterns, daily routines, relationships, package deliveries, comings and goings, and other behavioral patterns, making subjects unaware of the extent of observation and inference.
assumptions: Assumes the cloud service performs or can perform indexing, analytics, AI processing, or behavioral inference on stored clips.
uncertainty_note: Unawareness is inferred from typical opacity of downstream analytics; if the service clearly explains all processing, applicability may be reduced.

title: Cloud storage and secondary use of clips may exceed user expectations or consent
description: Users may expect clips to be stored only for backup or playback, while the destination may retain them longer, use them for service improvement, law-enforcement response, model training, or sharing with subprocessors without sufficiently specific consent or choice.
assumptions: Assumes purposes, retention, or onward sharing are broader than what users explicitly agreed to.
uncertainty_note: Consent/non-compliance depends on actual notices, legal basis, and controls; included as a plausible destination-side privacy threat for this flow.

title: Home Hub may disclose more motion-alert data than necessary to the backend
description: When forwarding a real-time motion alert, the Home Hub may include excessive personal data beyond what is strictly needed for alert handling, such as precise timestamps, continuous event streams, device identifiers, household identifiers, or contextual sensor details. Because motion events reveal occupancy and behavior patterns, unnecessary inclusion of such fields constitutes avoidable disclosure to another party in the system.
assumptions: The motion alert contains or can be linked to household/person-related information and the backend does not strictly require all transmitted fields for its purpose.

title: Motion-alert payload or flow metadata may identify the household or user in transit
description: The real-time alert and its associated metadata on this process-to-process flow may directly or indirectly identify a specific household, resident, or device owner. Even if the payload is minimized, identifiers, routing information, stable device IDs, account references, or distinctive timing patterns in transit can enable identification.
assumptions: The flow carries stable identifiers or metadata that can be associated with a specific account, device, or household.
uncertainty_note: Tree node citation is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include the Identification subtree.

title: Repeated motion alerts may be linkable to the same household over time
description: A stream of real-time motion alerts can allow events to be linked together as belonging to the same home, device, or account through persistent identifiers, network metadata, or recurring transmission patterns. This enables construction of occupancy and behavior profiles even if each individual alert appears limited.
assumptions: Alerts are associated with persistent identifiers or otherwise stable metadata across transmissions.
uncertainty_note: Tree node citation is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include the Linkability subtree.

title: Backend may expose motion alerts to more internal or external parties than necessary
description: Upon receipt, the mobile app backend may process, store, or onward-share motion alerts in ways that expose sensitive occupancy information to additional services, operators, analytics components, or third parties beyond what is necessary for delivering the alert. This broadening of involved parties increases avoidable disclosure risk.
assumptions: The backend stores or redistributes alert data to supporting services or personnel, and not all such exposure is strictly necessary.

title: Backend use of motion alerts may exceed the user's expected purpose
description: Users are likely to expect motion alerts to be used for immediate notification and security functionality. If the backend uses received alerts for secondary purposes such as analytics, profiling, service improvement, or model training without clear alignment to the original purpose, the processing becomes insufficiently transparent and potentially unexpected.
assumptions: The backend may retain and repurpose motion-alert data beyond immediate alert delivery.
uncertainty_note: Tree node citation is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include the Unawareness subtree.

title: Notification content discloses occupancy/activity information
description: By pushing a motion-detected alert to the homeowner, the backend shares information that can reveal presence, absence, or activity patterns at the home. If the notification text is overly specific (e.g., includes time, camera/location, or repeated event details), it may disclose sensitive behavior information beyond what is necessary.
assumptions: Assumes the push notification contains or implies that motion was detected at the residence and may include contextual details.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-effort based on generic disclosure of information; exact sub-node may vary by the project's threat-tree version.

title: Push-notification metadata can link homeowner identity to device/home events
description: Even if notification payloads are minimized or encrypted, metadata on the flow—such as device push token, timing, frequency, and routing via push infrastructure—can allow linking a specific homeowner/device to recurring motion events at a particular home.
assumptions: Assumes use of a mobile push-notification service where message delivery metadata is observable to intermediaries or service providers.
uncertainty_note: Exact observability depends on push-provider architecture and transport protections.

title: Notification delivery metadata may identify the homeowner or household
description: Identifiers used to deliver the notification, such as persistent device tokens, account identifiers, or stable routing metadata, may enable identification of the homeowner or their household when correlated with other data.
assumptions: Assumes persistent identifiers are used for push delivery and can be associated with a user account or household.
uncertainty_note: Identification may be indirect rather than explicit, depending on what identifiers are exposed to intermediaries.

title: Notification preview on the phone may disclose sensitive home-security events to bystanders
description: When the homeowner's device receives the motion alert, lock-screen previews, wearable mirroring, shared-device use, or visible banners can expose the fact that motion was detected at the home to nearby people, disclosing sensitive security and occupancy information.
assumptions: Assumes notifications may be displayed on lock screen or mirrored to companion devices by default.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is approximate; this is a destination-side disclosure caused by device presentation behavior.

title: The homeowner may be unaware of notification visibility and downstream exposure
description: The recipient may not understand that receiving the alert can expose motion-event details through lock-screen previews, notification history, or third-party device integrations, reducing their ability to make informed privacy choices about how alerts are presented.
assumptions: Assumes the app or platform does not clearly explain notification visibility settings and related privacy implications.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on the app's transparency and onboarding around notification privacy settings.

title: Backend shares analytics that may still be linkable to individual users or devices
description: Although described as aggregated device-usage analytics, the backend's act of disclosing the dataset to the analytics vendor can enable linking of records to the same device, account, household, or cohort if aggregation is too granular or stable identifiers, timestamps, rare combinations, or small-group statistics are included.
assumptions: Assumes the shared analytics may contain persistent pseudonyms, fine-grained timestamps, small-cell aggregates, or other quasi-identifiers rather than being strongly anonymized.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort because the retrieved context only confirmed applicable threat types/positions, not detailed node mappings.

title: Backend disclosure may permit inference of user or device identity from aggregated analytics
description: The backend may disclose analytics that, while not directly identifying, allow the vendor to identify or single out users/devices through rare usage patterns, geography, timing, or combination with other datasets already held by the vendor.
assumptions: Assumes aggregation is not sufficient to prevent singling out or re-identification when combined with auxiliary data.
uncertainty_note: Detailed threat-tree node selection is approximate.

title: Data flow metadata can link the app operator and analytics vendor relationship
description: Even if payload contents are aggregated, the existence, timing, frequency, volume, and routing metadata of this transfer can reveal a stable relationship between the mobile app backend and the analytics vendor and may support linkage of analytics batches to campaigns, releases, or user cohorts.
assumptions: Assumes network or transfer metadata is observable to relevant parties or retained by intermediaries.
uncertainty_note: Applies to flow metadata rather than payload content; node id is approximate.

title: Vendor can link received analytics with its other customer or platform data
description: Upon receipt, the cloud analytics vendor may correlate the shared analytics with other datasets it controls, enabling linkage across apps, services, devices, or time periods beyond the original context of collection.
assumptions: Assumes the vendor has additional datasets or identifiers enabling cross-context correlation.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node citation is best-effort.

title: Vendor may identify users, devices, or groups from the analytics
description: The analytics vendor may use auxiliary information, proprietary graphs, or historical telemetry to infer the identity of individuals, devices, or narrowly defined groups represented in the shared analytics.
assumptions: Assumes the vendor has sufficient side information and the shared data is not irreversibly anonymized.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate.

title: Vendor can learn sensitive behavior patterns from usage analytics
description: The received analytics may disclose habits, interests, routines, feature usage, location-related patterns, or other sensitive behavioral information about users or cohorts, even when aggregated.
assumptions: Assumes the analytics dimensions include behaviorally meaningful categories and sufficiently small or specific cohorts.
uncertainty_note: Threat applicability depends on the granularity and subject matter of the analytics.

title: Secondary analytics use by the vendor may exceed user expectations
description: The vendor may process the shared analytics for its own product improvement, benchmarking, model training, profiling, or cross-client insights in ways users did not expect when using the mobile app.
assumptions: Assumes contractual or technical controls do not strictly limit the vendor to a narrow processor role.
uncertainty_note: This is a common risk for third-party analytics sharing, but actual applicability depends on the vendor agreement and notices.

title: Sharing aggregated analytics with a third-party vendor may be insufficiently transparent or lack valid legal basis
description: If users were not clearly informed that their device-usage analytics would be shared with an external analytics vendor, or if consent/other legal basis does not cover this disclosure and downstream processing, the transfer may violate transparency, purpose-limitation, or lawful-processing requirements.
assumptions: Assumes applicable privacy law or policy requires notice, consent, contract terms, or other safeguards for this disclosure.
uncertainty_note: Compliance conclusions are jurisdiction- and implementation-specific; node id is approximate.

description: Metadata on the retrieval flow (for example homeowner account identifier, device/app identifiers, clip identifier, timestamps, IP address, and repeated access patterns) could allow observers of the flow or intermediaries handling the transfer to link multiple playback requests to the same household or person, even if the video payload itself is protected.
assumptions: Assumes the flow exposes stable identifiers or observable metadata to network intermediaries, logs, or monitoring components.

description: The retrieval request/response may contain or reveal identifiers that directly or indirectly identify the homeowner or household, such as account IDs, clip URLs, signed object references, IP address correlation, or highly distinctive timing/location patterns associated with playback.
assumptions: Assumes identifiers or quasi-identifiers are present in protocol fields, URLs, headers, logs, or observable traffic metadata.

description: By retrieving specific stored clips for playback, the mobile app backend can infer private information about the homeowner, such as when they were home, what events occurred, occupancy routines, visitors, or incidents of concern.
